title: How a Language Model Uses Context
subtitle: Tokens, context windows, and evidence

scenes.title: Start with a small question
scenes.body: The model sees the text supplied to this turn.
scenes.narration: Suppose you ask, “How does our order validator work?” The name sounds specific to us because we have the repository open. Look at the request, though. It contains neither a function nor a file reference. The assistant might search if this session can read the workspace. Before trusting the explanation, find the source it actually used.

scenes.result:

scenes.title: Text enters as tokens
scenes.body: A token can represent a word, part of a word, or punctuation.
scenes.narration: Look at the return line. A model reads pieces of this text called tokens. In this illustration, the space before quantity travels with the word, and the operator is another piece. Tokenizers can split the same line differently. That matters when you're estimating how much source, test output, and conversation can fit in a request.
scenes.code:
Text: return quantity > 0
Possible pieces, for illustration:
[return] [ quantity] [ >] [ 0]
scenes.result: A token count depends on the tokenizer.
scenes.action: Compare the phrase with the sample token split.

scenes.title: See what can fit
scenes.body: The context window is a finite token budget for a request.
scenes.narration: Picture the next request after a long debugging chat. It can include instructions, parts of the conversation, selected files, and tool results. The client chooses what to include within a finite budget. If you need the current condition to be available, attach the small source file. Then check whether the answer points back to that file.

scenes.title: Attach the actual function
scenes.body: The implementation determines the answer for this repository.
scenes.narration: Open order quantity dot pie in the training repository. Attach it in Copilot chat and ask what happens for zero and one. Read the return expression with me. Zero is equal to zero, so it passes. One is greater than zero, so it passes too. The code explains the observed behavior. We still need the issue to decide whether that behavior is correct.
scenes.result:
0 returns True because 0 >= 0.
1 returns True because 1 >= 0.
scenes.focus: Zero and one both return true
scenes.action: Attach order_quantity.py and trace both values.

scenes.title: Check the boundary
scenes.body: Run the same check in your approved training environment.
scenes.narration: Now check the explanation against the original training code. In an approved runner, call the function for zero and negative one. The output shows true for zero and false for negative one. That agrees with the comparison you read. If the result differs in another run, compare the checkout and confirm which version of the function you executed.
scenes.code:
python -B - <<'PY'
from order_quantity import is_valid_quantity
for n in (0, -1):
    print(n, is_valid_quantity(n))
PY
scenes.focus: The runner prints zero true and negative one false
scenes.action: Run the shown check in an approved runner.
